Narcissus
nar-SIS-us
proper noun
From the Greek Narkissos, the name of a flower and, in Greek legend, of a youth, thought to be connected with nárke, “numbness, torpor.” It was borne by a Roman householder whose people in the Lord are greeted by the apostle Paul in Romans 16:11.

See also: Narcissus

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Narcissus is known to us solely through a single greeting, in which the apostle Paul salutes “them which are of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord,” Romans 16:11. The words are carefully chosen, for the apostle does not necessarily greet Narcissus himself, but those of his household who are in the Lord — the believing servants and members of a great man’s house at Rome. Here is a precious thing: that within the establishment of a wealthy or notable Roman, whose own standing before God is not affirmed, there was a company of the redeemed, slaves it may be, and dependents, who had been called out of darkness into the marvellous light of Christ and gathered into His church. The gospel had entered under that roof and claimed its own, not the master perhaps, but the servants; not the great, but the lowly whom God delights to choose, 1 Corinthians 1:26. That Paul knew them, named them, and joined them to the fellowship of the saints at Rome shows the care of Christ for the least and most obscure of His people. The household of Narcissus reminds us that grace runs where it will, plucking believers even from the houses of the powerful, and that the true company of the faithful is often the hidden remnant “in the Lord” within a house that does not own His name.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Roman householder whose members in the Lord are greeted by Paul in Romans 16:11.

NARCISSUS, proper noun. A man at Rome named once in Scripture, in the greetings of the sixteenth chapter of Romans.

The head of a household within which were believers, saluted by the apostle Paul.

Not himself necessarily greeted, but “them which are of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord.”

A witness that the gospel gathered its own even within the houses of the notable at Rome.

A name that marks the hidden company of the faithful within a great man’s establishment.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:11 — "Salute them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord."

1Co 1:26 — "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called."

Phi 4:22 — "All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household."

1Pe 2:9 — "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A hidden company of believers, not a contested doctrine; the household of Narcissus recovers the reach of grace into the houses of the great.

expand to see more

Narcissus is a name upon which nothing rests but a single greeting, and there is nothing in it for the age to redefine; he is simply the head of a Roman house within which the gospel had found and claimed a believing company.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle this brief mention recovers is the free and searching reach of sovereign grace, which calls not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble, 1 Corinthians 1:26, but plucks its own even from the households of the powerful — servants and dependents made a chosen generation, called out of darkness into His marvellous light. As Paul could greet the saints of Caesar’s own household, Philippians 4:22, so he greets the believers under the roof of Narcissus, teaching us that the true church is often a hidden remnant “in the Lord” within a house that does not own His name, and that no establishment, however great, is beyond the entrance of the gospel.
